You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'SyncBoost_Rectifier': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 2c7f143a90f6).

what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -8 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -56 % of the load's need on S4 (weak excitation), -18 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{avg} \ge 1.8V$, $V_{max} \le 3.6V$, $V_{pp} \le 0.02V$, $t_{up} \le 0.15s$, $dv \le 0.01V$.
    *   Current Best: `SSHI_FullBridge` (topology `40eae91a637a`).
    *   `SSHI_FullBridge` results: $V_{avg}$ is good, $V_{max}$ is good, $t_{up}$ is good, $dv$ is good.
    *   Main failure: $V_{pp}$ (ripple) is too high (e.g., 67-92 mV, needs $\le 20$ mV).
    *   The ripple is primarily caused by the small output capacitance ($C_1 \approx 416\text{ nF}$) not being able to smooth the charge pulses.
    *   S4 is very close on ripple (21 mV).

    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` is a hybrid: an SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) for voltage flipping, followed by a full-bridge rectifier.
    *   The ripple failure is a capacitor sizing issue, but the optimizer might be hitting a limit or the interaction with $t_{up}$ (startup time) is limiting the capacitor size. Larger $C_{out}$ increases $t_{up}$ because it takes longer to charge.
    *   Actually, if $C_1$ is $416\text{ nF}$ and ripple is $67\text{ mV}$ with $R_L = 330\text{ k}\Omega$, the energy pulses are quite large.

    *   The ripple failure suggests we need a larger $C_{out}$. However, if the optimizer already tried values up to $4.7\mu\text{F}$ (the component limit) and still failed, there might be an issue. Let's check the current value: $4.16\text{ e-07}$ (416 nF). This is quite small. The limit is $4.7\mu\text{F}$. The optimizer should have been able to increase it.
    *   Wait, why didn't it increase $C_{out}$? Possibly because $t_{up}$ (startup) would exceed $0.15\text{s}$.
    *   $t_{up}$ for `SSHI_FullBridge` is $0.04\text{s}$ to $0.12\text{s}$. If it increases $C_{out}$ by 10x to reduce ripple by 10x, $t_{up}$ would likely increase by 10x, exceeding $0.15\text{s}$.
    *   So, the trade-off is: $C_{out}$ must be large enough for ripple, but small enough for startup.
    *   To allow a larger $C_{out}$ while maintaining $t_{up}$, we need more charge per cycle or a more efficient transfer.

    *   SSHI usually improves voltage flipping $\rightarrow$ higher average voltage $\rightarrow$ faster charging.
    *   Is there a way to get better ripple without just increasing $C_{out}$?
    *   Active ripple cancellation? (Too complex for 16 components).
    *   Low-dropout regulation? (Need more components).
    *   A better SSHI implementation? The current `SSHI_FullBridge` has L and S in parallel with the piezo? No, the provided components are:
        `L1 L pzp n1 0.00785`, `S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1`, `D1...D4` bridge.
        This looks like an SSHI circuit where the inductor is used to flip the piezo voltage.
    *   Wait, if the ripple is the only issue, perhaps a "Pseudo-SSHI" or a different inductor placement could help? Or simply a more optimized SSHI.
    *   Let's try a standard SSHI with a different bridge configuration or a charge pump.

    *   The current `SSHI_FullBridge` is:
        - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
        - L1 from pzp to n1
        - S1 from n1 to pzn
        - Rectifier (D1-D4) from pzp/pzn to out.
    *   This is essentially flipping the voltage on the piezo.
    *   The problem is that we are charging the output capacitor $C_{out}$ through the bridge diodes in bursts.

    *   Maybe a "Synchronous Rectifier" would be more efficient? But we only have 4 switches.
    *   Let's try a "Buck-Boost" or "Boost" converter based on the piezo.
    *   Wait, the `SyncBoost_Rectifier` failed the screen.
    *   Let's look at a "Parallel SSHI" or "Symmetric SSHI".

    *   Symmetric SSHI often uses two inductors and two switches to flip the voltage more effectively.
    *   Connectivity:
        - L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1, S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn
        - L2: pzn $\rightarrow$ n2, S2: n2 $\rightarrow$ pzp
        - Rectifier: D1, D2 from pzp/pzn to out.
        - This is more complex.

    *   What if we use a simple bridge but improve the charging?
    *   Actually, let's look at the ripple again. $V_{pp}$ is the peak-to-peak ripple in the *final* window (0.7-0.8s).
    *   If the ripple is 67mV and we need 20mV, we need $C_{out}$ to be roughly 3-4 times larger.
    *   If $C_{out}$ becomes $1.5\mu\text{F}$ to $2\mu\text{F}$, $t_{up}$ might exceed $0.15\text{s}$.
    *   Is there a way to speed up $t_{up}$?
    *   SSHI is already quite fast. Maybe the `phase` or `ton` can be tuned better? (The optimizer does that).

    *   Let's try a topology that decouples the charge delivery from the output capacitor to some extent, or provides higher peak currents.
    *   What about a "Charge Pump" (Dickson or similar)? Not great for piezo.

    *   Let's try a "Symmetric SSHI" (SECE-like).
    *   Wait, `SECE_Symmetric` was already explored (hash `fcb6f6a8b4de`) and it was not as good.

    *   What if we use a "Voltage Doubler" approach?
    *   D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
    *   C1: n1 $\rightarrow$ 0
    *   D2: n1 $\rightarrow$ out
    *   (This is a basic half-wave doubler).

    *   Let's rethink the SSHI. The standard SSHI (inductor-based) is:
        1. Piezo charges $C_{out}$ through diode.
        2. At peak, switch closes, $L$ flips $V_{piezo}$.
        3. Piezo charges $C_{out}$ again.
    *   The current `SSHI_FullBridge` has a full bridge. A full bridge is more efficient than a half-bridge.

    *   Wait! The current `SSHI_FullBridge` uses `D1 D pzp out DSCH`, `D2 D pzn out DSCH`, `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`, `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`.
    *   This is a full bridge.
    *   If I want to reduce ripple without increasing $t_{up}$ too much, I need to increase the *average* current delivered during the charge phase.
    *   Maybe a different inductor configuration?

    *   The ripple failure is very consistent. $V_{pp}$ is around 60-90mV.
    *   $V_{pp} \approx \Delta Q / C_{out}$.
    *   $\Delta Q$ is the charge delivered in one pulse.
    *   If $V_{avg} \approx 2.8\text{V}$, $R_L = 330\text{k}\Omega$, $I_{load} = 8.5\mu\text{A}$.
    *   In one period ($T = 10\text{ms}$), $Q_{load} = 8.5\mu\text{A} \times 10\text{ms} = 85\text{nC}$.
    *   For $V_{pp} = 20\text{mV}$, $C_{out} = 85\text{nC} / 0.02\text{V} = 4.25\mu\text{F}$.
    *   So the optimizer *should* have tried $C_{out} \approx 4\mu\text{F}$.
    *   If $C_{out} = 4\mu\text{F}$, $t_{up} \approx (1.8\text{V} \times 4\mu\text{F}) / I_{avg}$.
    *   $I_{avg}$ for S1 is $P_{load}/V_{avg} = 23.1\mu\text{W} / 2.76\text{V} \approx 8.3\mu\text{A}$.
    *   $t_{up} \approx 7.2\mu\text{C} / 8.3\mu\text{A} \approx 0.86\text{s}$.
    *   SURELY $t_{up}$ will fail if $C_{out}$ is large!
    *   This is the core problem: $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$ is a very tight constraint.
    *   To get $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$ with $C_{out} = 4\mu\text{F}$, we need $I_{avg} \ge 7.2\mu\text{C} / 0.15\text{s} = 48\mu\text{A}$.
    *   But the load $I_{load}$ is only $8-20\mu\text{A}$. The energy comes from the piezo.
    *   $I_{piezo\_peak} = 50\mu\text{A}$. The average rectified current is much lower.

    *   Wait, if $C_{out}$ must be small for $t_{up}$, but large for ripple, how can any circuit pass?
    *   The only way is if the charge is delivered *more continuously* rather than in large pulses.
    *   Standard rectifier: pulses every $T/2$.
    *   If we can deliver charge more frequently or in smaller, more frequent packets, ripple decreases.
    *   Or, use a secondary filter?
    *   Example: $C_{out}$ (large) $\rightarrow$ $R_{filter}$ $\rightarrow$ $C_{load}$ (small).
    *   But $R_{filter}$ would drop voltage.
    *   Alternatively, use a switch-capacitor filter? (Too many components).

    *   What if we use a "Buck" converter?
    *   $V_{piezo} \rightarrow$ L $\rightarrow$ S $\rightarrow$ Out.
    *   A buck converter can deliver current more continuously.
    *   But we only have one `SYNC` controller and one switch for the buck.
    *   Wait, the `SYNC` controller can operate at the piezo frequency. A buck converter at 100Hz will still have ripple.

    *   Let's look at the `SyncBoost_Rectifier` again. It used a boost approach.
    *   What about a "Boost" converter with a very high switching frequency? No, `SYNC` only triggers at piezo extrema.

    *   Is there another way to reduce ripple?
    *   Maybe a "Capacitor-based" SSHI? (No, we have inductors).
    *   What if we use a very small $C_{out}$ for $t_{up}$ and a *zener-based* regulator to clip $V_{max}$ and then a large $C_{load}$? No, the load is $R_L$ and it's connected to `out`.

    *   Let's reconsider the $t_{up}$ constraint.
    *   $t_{up} = 0.15\text{s}$.
    *   If we use a very small $C_{out}$ to start, and then... no, the capacitor is fixed.
    *   Is it possible to charge $C_{out}$ faster?
    *   The energy available per cycle is $E = \frac{1}{2} C_p (V_{oc}^2)$.
    *   $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}, C_p = 25\text{nF} \rightarrow E \approx 128\text{ pJ}$.
    *   Wait, $128\text{ pJ}$ per half cycle? $25.6\text{ nJ}$ per second.
    *   $P = 25.6\text{ nW}$. This is way too low.
    *   Let's re-calculate $V_{oc}$. $I_p = 50\mu\text{A}, f = 100\text{Hz}, C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
    *   $V_{oc} = I_p / (2 \pi f C_p) = 50\mu\text{A} / (2 \pi \times 100 \times 25\text{nF}) = 50\mu\text{A} / 15.7\text{nS} \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
    *   $E_{cycle} = \int I \cdot V dt \approx \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 \times 2 \text{ (per cycle)} = 25\text{nF} \times (3.18)^2 \approx 250\text{nJ}$.
    *   $P_{avg} = 250\text{nJ} \times 100\text{Hz} = 25\mu\text{W}$.
    *   This matches the $P_{load}$ seen in the results ($\sim 20\mu\text{W}$).

    *   Okay, so $P_{avg} \approx 25\mu\text{W}$.
    *   To charge $C_{out} = 4\mu\text{F}$ to $1.8\text{V}$:
    *   $E_{stored} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4\mu\text{F} \times (1.8\text{V})^2 = 6.48\mu\text{J}$.
    *   $t_{up} = E_{stored} / P_{avg} = 6.48\mu\text{J} / 25\mu\text{W} = 0.259\text{s}$.
    *   This is still $> 0.15\text{s}$.
    *   So even with 100% efficiency, a $4\mu\text{F}$ capacitor takes $0.26\text{s}$ to charge to $1.8\text{V}$.
    *   But we need $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{s}$.
    *   This means $C_{out}$ *must* be smaller than $\approx 2\mu\text{F}$.
    *   If $C_{out} \le 2\mu\text{F}$, then $V_{pp} = Q_{load} / C_{out} = 85\text{nC} / 2\mu\text{F} = 42.5\text{mV}$.
    *   Still $> 20\text{mV}$.

    *   Is there any way to reduce ripple without increasing $C_{out}$?
    *   Yes, if the charge is delivered more frequently.
    *   A full-bridge rectifier delivers charge twice per cycle (every $5\text{ms}$).
    *   If we could deliver it 4 times per cycle... or use a different topology.
    *   What if we use a "Charge Pump" that works on the edges?
    *   Actually, what if we use a small $C_{out}$ for startup, and a *separate* larger capacitor for ripple?
    *   Wait, the goal says "storage capacitor at node 'out'". The load $R_L$ is also at node 'out'.
    *   If I put a resistor between $C_{storage}$ and $C_{out}$, the $V_{avg}$ will drop.
    *   But what if the "resistor" is a switch?
    *   No, that's too complex.

    *   Wait! Let's look at the `SSHI_FullBridge` results again.
    *   S4 ripple was $21\text{mV}$. $C_{out}$ was $416\text{nF}$.
    *   S4 is "weak excitation" ($I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$) and "light load" ($R_L = 2.2\text{M}\Omega$).
    *   $I_{load\_S4} = 1.98\text{V} / 2.2\text{M}\Omega \approx 0.9\mu\text{A}$.
    *   $Q_{load\_S4} = 0.9\mu\text{A} \times 10\text{ms} = 9\text{nC}$.
    *   $V_{pp\_S4} = 9\text{nC} / 416\text{nF} \approx 21.6\text{mV}$.
    *   This matches the result.

    *   So for S1 ($R_L = 330\text{k}\Omega$), $I_{load\_S1} = 2.76\text{V} / 330\text{k}\Omega \approx 8.3\mu\text{A}$.
    *   $Q_{load\_S1} = 83\text{nC}$.
    *   $V_{pp\_S1} = 83\text{nC} / 416\text{nF} \approx 200\text{mV}$. (Wait, the result says 67mV).
    *   Why is it 67mV and not 200mV?
    *   Ah, because the charge is delivered twice per cycle.
    *   $\Delta V = Q_{half-cycle} / C_{out} = (8.3\mu\text{A} \times 5\text{ms}) / 416\text{nF} = 41.5\text{nC} / 416\text{nF} \approx 100\text{mV}$.
    *   Still a bit higher than 67mV, but closer.

    *   Conclusion: To pass ripple, we *must* have a larger $C_{out}$. To pass $t_{up}$, we *must* charge it faster.
    *   How to charge $C_{out}$ faster?
    *   SSHI is already the fastest way to extract energy from a piezo.
    *   Is there any other way?
    *   Maybe by using a *smaller* $C_{out}$ but a *very* low-impedance path? No, $C_{out}$ is the storage.
    *   What if we use a "Current Doubler" or something? No.

    *   Let's try one more thing: a different SSHI variant.
    *   Some SSHI circuits use a switch and a capacitor instead of an inductor.
    *   But we have inductors.

    *   What if we use the "Symmetric SSHI" but with a better rectifier?
    *   Symmetric SSHI (using two inductors) can flip the voltage more completely.
    *   Actually, the `SSHI_FullBridge` already used an inductor to flip.
    *   Let's try to implement a "Synchronous Rectifier" to reduce the diode drop.
